q: Why do traditional fully connected networks cope poorly with images?
options: They do not use local groups of neighbouring pixels that form shapes
They cannot apply a nonlinear function to neuron outputs
They cannot be trained using backpropagation at all
They only accept grayscale images with a single channel
explain: The meaning of an image sits in groups of neighbouring pixels, and a fully connected network does not use that local structure. It can still use nonlinear functions and backpropagation, so those options fail.

q: What does a channel refer to in a digital image?
options: A hidden layer between the input and the output of a network
A class label that the network can assign to a picture
A colour component of the image, stored as a 2D matrix
A filter position as the kernel slides across the image
explain: A colour image is like three 2D matrices stacked together, one each for red, green and blue. A grayscale image has just one channel.

q: In a convolutional layer, what is the job of a filter, also called a kernel?
options: It randomly switches off outputs to stop the network memorising
It slides over the input to detect features such as edges
It converts feature values into probabilities that sum to one
It rescales pixel values so that features share a similar size
explain: The filter holds weights that are multiplied with each patch of the input, so it acts as a feature detector. Switching off outputs is dropout and turning values into probabilities is softmax.

q: Which tasks can different filters carry out on an input image?
options: Randomly dropping layer outputs
Converting logits into class probabilities
Detecting edges
Softening the image
Sharpening the image
Detecting corners
explain: Different kernels pull out different features and can also sharpen or soften an image. Producing probabilities belongs to the softmax layer and dropping outputs belongs to the dropout layer.

q: A kernel is moved across an image with a stride of 2 instead of 1. What is the effect?
options: The kernel doubles in size and covers more of the image
The border of the image is filled with zeros first
Each kernel weight is doubled, so features get stronger
The kernel moves two positions per step, so the output is smaller
explain: Stride is the amount the kernel shifts over the input. A bigger shift means fewer positions are visited. Filling the border with zeros describes padding, not stride.

q: Why is padding added around the border of an image before convolution?
options: To enlarge the kernel so it can detect bigger shapes
To convert a colour image into a single channel image
To handle edge pixels, which the kernel would otherwise cover less
To increase the stride so the kernel moves faster
explain: A sliding kernel treats pixels at the edges differently from the rest, so a border is added. Padding does not change the kernel size, the number of channels or the stride.

q: Which of these are forms of padding?
options: Reflection padding
Replication padding
Dropout padding
Softmax padding
Zero padding
explain: Zero padding fills the border with zeros, and reflection and replication padding fill it using the image's own edge values. Dropout and softmax are separate layer types, not padding methods.
flag: Slide 16 is image only, so the padding types come from the text on slide 15.

q: How do the filters of a CNN become useful feature detectors?
options: They start random and are refined by feedforward and backpropagation
They are designed by hand to match edges and corners
They are copied from the pooling layer after training
They stay at their random starting values during training
explain: Filters are randomly initialised like ordinary weights and biases, then repeated training evolves them into strong feature extractors. They are not hand designed and they do not stay random.

q: A max pooling layer is added after a convolutional layer. What is its main job?
options: To enlarge the feature maps so finer detail is recovered
To turn the feature maps into a single vector
To randomly ignore some outputs so the network cannot memorise
To shrink the feature maps while keeping the dominant features
explain: Pooling shrinks the convolved features, which lowers the computing needed. Turning maps into a vector is the flatten layer and ignoring outputs at random is dropout.

q: A kernel covers a patch of values in a feature map. How does average pooling summarise that patch?
options: It keeps only the largest value in the patch
It returns the mean of all the values in the patch
It keeps the first value that the kernel reaches
It subtracts the patch mean from every value
explain: Average pooling returns the average of the values under the kernel. Keeping only the largest value describes max pooling, which is the tempting wrong choice.

q: Which are benefits of a pooling layer?
options: It extracts dominant features that are rotation and position invariant
It shrinks the spatial size of the convolved features
It helps keep the training of the model effective
It lowers the computing power needed to process the data
explain: Pooling reduces dimensions, saves computation and keeps dominant features that do not depend on exact position or rotation, which supports effective training. All four statements are correct.

q: What does an activation layer do in a CNN?
options: It gates a neuron's output, deciding whether it is activated
It slides a kernel over the image to extract local features
It averages groups of neighbouring values to shrink the map
It flattens the feature maps into one long vector
explain: An activation function is a gate that decides what a neuron outputs. In a CNN it is applied across the two dimensions of each feature map. ReLU is the most popular choice.

q: Why are input features scaled to a similar range, such as 0 to 1?
options: So that the output layer produces probabilities that sum to one
So that the image shrinks before pooling is applied
So that each feature contributes about equally to the prediction
So that neurons can be dropped at random during training
explain: Normalisation makes feature sizes comparable, so one feature with large values does not dominate. Producing probabilities is softmax, and dropping neurons is dropout.

q: Batches from a dataset look very different from each other, and training keeps swinging between them. What is this problem called?
options: Overfitting, where training error is tiny but error on new data is large
Covariate shift, a large change in data distribution between batches
Underfitting, where training error stays high however long training runs
Vanishing gradient, where early layers barely update at all
explain: When batches differ a lot, the network keeps changing its weights towards each odd distribution, which slows training. Batch normalisation reduces this. Overfitting is about memorising the training set instead.

q: Which statements about batch normalisation are correct?
options: It works on the feature maps of a mini batch
It generally speeds up learning and leads to faster convergence
For each feature it subtracts the mini batch mean and divides by the mini batch standard deviation
It chooses the largest value from each patch of the feature map
It randomly removes outputs to reduce memorisation
explain: Batch normalisation standardises each feature using mini batch statistics, which speeds up learning. Removing outputs at random is dropout and taking the largest value is max pooling.

q: Which statements describe overfitting?
options: The error on new data is large
The error on the training set becomes very small
The network generalises well to new situations
The error on the training set stays high however long training runs
explain: An overfitted network has memorised the training examples, so training error is tiny but new data gives large error. It has not learned to generalise.

q: How does dropout reduce overfitting during training?
options: It permanently deletes the weakest neurons after the first pass
It normalises each feature using the mini batch mean and variance
It reduces the spatial size of the feature maps in each layer
It randomly ignores some layer outputs, so the layer differs on each pass
explain: Dropout is a regularisation technique that randomly drops outputs during training, so the network cannot rely on memorising everything. The dropped outputs are not removed for good.

q:
Is the following statement correct?
"Dropout is used so that a network can memorise the whole training set."
options: Yes, because dropout stores the training examples inside the layer
Yes, because dropping outputs makes the layer more accurate on training data only
No, because dropout is a regularisation technique that stops memorising
No, because dropout is only used to shrink the size of feature maps
explain: The purpose of dropout is the opposite of memorisation. By ignoring random outputs it pushes the network to generalise. Shrinking feature maps is the job of pooling.

q: What are the two main stages of a CNN?
options: Convolution and pooling to find features, then fully connected layers to predict the label
Fully connected layers to find features, then convolution and pooling to predict the label
Normalisation to prepare the image, then pooling to predict the label
Pooling to find features, then convolution to predict the label
explain: The first stage breaks the image into features and analyses them. The second stage, made of fully connected layers, uses those features to predict the best label.

q: What does the flatten layer at the start of the fully connected stage do?
options: It gives the final probability for each label using softmax
It applies a filter to detect edges in the image
It randomly drops outputs to prevent overfitting
It turns the earlier output into one vector for the next stage
explain: The flatten layer takes the feature maps and turns them into one vector so that ordinary fully connected layers can use them. Final probabilities come from the softmax output layer.

q: What is the purpose of the softmax function in the output layer?
options: It flattens feature maps into a single vector
It turns raw values, called logits, into probabilities summing to one
It decides which neuron outputs to drop at random
It scales each feature to the range 0 to 1 across a mini batch
explain: Softmax gives the final probability for each label, and the probabilities add up to one. Flattening, dropout and batch normalisation are different layers.

q: Which are types of fully connected layer in a CNN?
options: A softmax layer that acts as the output
A pooling input layer that keeps the maximum
A normal layer that applies weights and biases
A flatten layer that acts as the input
A convolutional output layer that applies a small kernel
explain: Fully connected layers include the flatten input layer, ordinary layers with weights and biases, and the softmax output layer. Kernels and maximum values belong to convolution and pooling.

q: Which statements about convolution are correct?
options: It returns the maximum value from each patch
Its filters start random and improve through training
Its filters are designed by hand and then frozen
The most common filter size is 3 by 3
It multiplies a set of weights with the input in a linear operation
explain: Convolution is a linear operation between a filter and the input, filters are learned, and 3 by 3 is the usual size. Hand designed frozen filters and maximum values do not describe it.

q: Explain why a traditional fully connected network does not scale well to images and what a CNN assumes instead.
model: The meaning of an image sits in groups of neighbouring pixels that together form a shape, and a traditional network is not designed to use these local features. It treats pixels as separate inputs, so it is good at classifying but poor at extracting features. A CNN assumes the input is an image. This lets the architecture encode visual features and use local patterns, so it extracts features better and runs more efficiently.
points: Image meaning comes from groups of neighbouring pixels
Traditional networks do not use local features and are weak at feature extraction
A CNN assumes the input is an image
So a CNN uses local features and works more efficiently

q: Describe what the convolution operation does and the role of the filter.
model: Convolution slides a small 2D array of weights, called a filter or kernel, over the image and multiplies it with each patch of input. This is a linear operation that extracts and keeps local features. Different filters pick out different features such as edges or corners. The result is a smaller output that is easier to process without losing features that matter for prediction. The filters begin random and are improved by training.
points: A filter or kernel is a 2D array of weights applied across the input
It multiplies the weights with each patch of input in a linear operation
Different filters detect different features such as edges and corners
The output is smaller but keeps the features that matter
Filters start random and are learned in training

q: Explain what stride and padding control in a convolution.
model: Stride is the amount the kernel shifts each time as it moves across the input. It moves right by the stride until the width is covered, then drops down and repeats. A larger stride means fewer positions and a smaller output. Padding adds extra values around the border of the image so that edge pixels are handled properly. The most common choice is zero padding, but reflection and replication padding also exist.
points: Stride is the shift of the kernel at each step
A larger stride visits fewer positions
Padding adds a border to handle edge pixels
Zero padding is common and reflection or replication padding are alternatives

q: Compare max pooling and average pooling and explain why a CNN uses pooling.
model: A pooling layer reduces the spatial size of the convolved features, which lowers the computing power needed. It also extracts dominant features that do not depend much on position or rotation, which keeps training effective. Max pooling returns the largest value in the patch covered by the kernel. Average pooling returns the mean of all values in that patch. Max pooling keeps the strongest response while average pooling gives a smoother summary.
points: Pooling reduces spatial size and computation
It keeps dominant features that are position and rotation invariant
Max pooling returns the maximum value in the patch
Average pooling returns the mean of the patch

q: Explain the purpose of the activation layer in a CNN and name the most popular activation function.
model: An activation function is a mathematical equation that decides the output of a neuron. In a CNN it works across two dimensions like a screen and decides whether each output pixel is activated. It acts as a gate between the inputs feeding a neuron and its output going to the next layer. It also adds the nonlinearity that a plain dot product lacks. ReLU is the most popular activation function in CNNs.
points: It decides the output of a neuron
It acts as a gate between inputs and output
It decides whether each output pixel is activated
ReLU is the most popular choice
flag: The nonlinearity point is standard textbook knowledge. Slide 4 only says the dot product is optionally followed by a nonlinearity.

q: Explain how batch normalisation helps the training of a CNN.
model: Very different looking batches cause a large shift in the data distribution, called covariate shift. The network is misled into changing its weights towards one odd batch, so it bounces between distributions and learns slowly. Batch normalisation works on feature maps across a mini batch. For each feature it finds the mean and variance, subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation. This speeds up learning and gives faster convergence.
points: Different batches cause covariate shift
Covariate shift slows training because the network bounces between distributions
It subtracts the mini batch mean and divides by the standard deviation for each feature
Learning is faster and converges sooner

q: Explain what overfitting is and how a dropout layer helps to prevent it.
model: Overfitting happens when the error on the training set is very small but the error on new data is large. The network has memorised the training examples and has not learned to generalise. Dropout is a simple regularisation technique. During training it randomly ignores some layer outputs, so the layer looks different from one pass to the next. This stops the network relying on memorising the whole training set.
points: Overfitting means tiny training error but large error on new data
The network has memorised rather than generalised
Dropout is a regularisation technique
It randomly ignores some layer outputs during training

q: Describe the role of the fully connected layers at the end of a CNN, including the flatten layer and softmax.
model: Once convolution and pooling have found features, fully connected layers use them to predict the best label for the image. The flatten layer first turns the feature maps into a single vector. Normal fully connected layers then apply weights and biases to the features. The output layer uses softmax, which turns the raw values, called logits, into a probability for each label. The probabilities sum to one.
points: They take the output of the feature stage and predict a label
Flatten turns feature maps into a single vector
Normal layers apply weights and biases
Softmax turns logits into probabilities that sum to one

q: Describe the layers of a CNN and the order in which an image moves through them to produce a label.
model: A typical CNN stacks layers that reduce the image size while keeping the features that separate one class from another. Convolutional layers apply filters to find local features. Activation layers act as gates on the outputs, normalisation layers keep feature values comparable, pooling layers shrink the maps and dropout layers fight overfitting. This is the feature stage. A flatten layer then feeds fully connected layers, and a softmax output layer gives the label probabilities.
points: Six layer types are convolution, pooling, activation, normalisation, dropout and fully connected
The feature stage reduces size while keeping key features
Flatten feeds the fully connected layers
Softmax gives the final label probabilities
